query: Review main.bicep before we ship it. It builds fine locally so CI passes, but the last deploy of a very similar template blew up in ARM and I never understood why. Tell me what is actually wrong and what to change.
expected_behavior: Identifies that `storageName` is built as `st-${workload}-${env}-${uniqueString(...)}`, which produces hyphens and roughly 30 characters, while a storage account name must be 3-24 characters of lowercase letters and digits only - and says explicitly that `bicep build` cannot catch this because resource name rules are enforced by ARM at deployment time, not by the compiler

Says the role assignment `name: '${workload}-owner-assignment'` is invalid because a `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments` name must be a GUID, and prescribes `guid(<scope id>, principalId, roleDefinitionId)` so that redeploying is idempotent rather than creating or colliding with a new assignment

Rejects Owner (`8e3af657-a8ff-443c-a75c-2fe8c4bcb635`) at resource-group scope for the site identity and replaces it with a data-plane role at the storage scope - `Storage Blob Data Contributor` (`ba92f5b4-2d11-453d-a403-e96b0029c9fe`) or narrower - noting the site has no identity block at all today

States that the template compiles with exit code 0 even though the linter reports `outputs-should-not-contain-secrets` and `secure-parameter-default`, because those rules default to warning level, and shows how to escalate them to `error` in `bicepconfig.json` under `analyzers.core.rules` so CI actually fails
Notes that `use-recent-api-versions` is disabled by default, so the 2021-era API versions in this file draw no diagnostic until the rule is switched on with a `maxAgeInDays` setting

Replaces the `resourceId()` / `listKeys(resourceId(...))` / `reference(...)` string plumbing with symbolic references (`plan.id`, `storage.listKeys()`, `site.identity.principalId`), and explains that this is what lets Bicep infer the dependency graph - which is why the explicit `dependsOn` block was needed in the first place and can then be deleted

Removes the storage key and SQL password from `appSettings` and from `output storageAccountKey`, because deployment outputs are stored in the resource group's deployment history and readable by anyone with read access, and moves the app to managed identity or Key Vault references instead

Flags `allowBlobPublicAccess: true` and the hardcoded `location = 'eastus'` default, and recommends Azure Verified Modules (`br/public:avm/res/...` pinned to an exact version) instead of hand-rolled resource blocks
Stays in Bicep and does not propose rewriting the template in Terraform

query: provision-aks.sh is what we were about to run for our first production cluster. Go through it and tell me what will hurt us, especially anything we cannot change after the cluster exists.
expected_behavior: Says `--network-plugin kubenet` is the legacy model and is being retired on March 31, 2028, and that the pod IP model cannot be changed in place on an existing cluster, so this is a create-time decision - recommends Azure CNI Overlay as the default, and names its 250-pods-per-node ceiling

Names **AKS Automatic** as the recommended production default rather than hand-tuning a Base-SKU cluster, and describes what it brings: Standard-tier cluster management preconfigured, Node Auto Provisioning, support for up to 5,000 nodes, and a pod readiness SLA on top of the API-server uptime SLA

Points out that `--tier free` carries no financially backed uptime SLA and is recommended only below about 10 nodes, while Standard gives 99.95% API-server availability with availability zones and 99.9% without, up to 5,000 nodes - and that the script deploys 2 nodes with no `--zones 1 2 3` at all

Warns that the script names no pod or service CIDR, so both are defaults that cannot be replaced after creation, and that AKS outright rejects ranges overlapping its reserved blocks - `169.254.0.0/16`, `192.0.2.0/24`, `172.30.0.0/16` and `172.31.0.0/16` - which is why an apparently ordinary `172.16.0.0/12` pod CIDR fails at creation

Replaces `--service-principal` / `--client-secret` with `--enable-managed-identity`, and replaces the ACR admin user and the `docker-registry` pull secret with the `AcrPull` role assignment that `--attach-acr` already creates for the kubelet identity

Calls out `az aks get-credentials --admin` as a cluster-admin certificate that bypasses Microsoft Entra entirely and cannot be audited per-user, and prescribes `--enable-aad --enable-azure-rbac` with ordinary (non-admin) credentials

Notes that the workload must reach an Azure SQL private endpoint in an existing VNet, but the script lets AKS create its own managed VNet - the cluster has to be created into that subnet with `--vnet-subnet-id`, another decision that cannot be changed afterwards

Rejects `Standard_B2s` burstable VMs for production nodes and asks for at least 4 vCPU non-burstable SKUs, and adds a dedicated system node pool tainted `CriticalAddonsOnly` separate from the user workloads

Treats the pinned `--kubernetes-version 1.29.4` as a liability: AKS supports only the three most recent minor versions, so the cluster needs `--auto-upgrade-channel` plus `--node-os-upgrade-channel` and a maintenance window rather than a version frozen in a script - and notes that extended support past community support means the Premium tier, which must be set together with `--k8s-support-plan AKSLongTermSupport`
Keeps the answer on the AKS control plane and does not start writing Deployment manifests, probes, resource limits or a Dockerfile

query: role-assignments.json is the access review export for our production subscription. Security wants this cleaned up before audit. What is actually dangerous here versus merely untidy?
expected_behavior: Reads `roleAssignmentsInSubscription: 4872` against the hard ceiling of 5000 role assignments per subscription, states that this limit is fixed and cannot be raised by a support request, and notes that management-group-scope and PIM-eligible assignments do not count toward it - so moving assignments up to a management group or onto Entra groups is the way out

Identifies that `Storage Account Contributor` is a management-plane role that does not grant access to blob data, so the app's stated job of reading and writing blobs either fails or is being done with account keys - the correct grant is `Storage Blob Data Contributor` scoped to the container

Identifies the same management-plane versus data-plane mistake on Key Vault: `Key Vault Contributor` manages the vault resource but does not read secrets, the app needs `Key Vault Secrets User`, and that replacement only takes effect if the vault has `enableRbacAuthorization` set - on an access-policy vault the role assignment is accepted and does nothing

Treats Owner at subscription scope for `sp-github-deploy` as the top finding, and removes the long-lived client secret in favour of workload identity federation (OIDC) from the CI provider, which issues short-lived tokens and has no secret to expire or leak
Notes that the Contributor assignment on `rg-orders-prod` for the same principal is redundant while Owner exists at the subscription above it, and is dead weight against the 5000 ceiling

Calls the `Orders Deployer` custom role with `actions: ["*"]` an Owner-equivalent role wearing a different name - `notActions` on `Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete` removes almost nothing, since write on role assignments is still granted

Flags the standing `User Access Administrator` assignment for a human at subscription scope, proposes making it PIM-eligible and time-bound rather than active, and names `Role Based Access Control Administrator` as the least-privilege alternative for anyone who only needs to manage role assignments

Gives the replacement grants as role definition GUIDs rather than display names - `ba92f5b4-2d11-453d-a403-e96b0029c9fe` for Storage Blob Data Contributor, `4633458b-17de-408a-b874-0445c86b69e6` for Key Vault Secrets User - because names are localised and IaC needs the ID
Stays on Azure RBAC and Microsoft Entra and does not drift into AWS IAM policies or Terraform code

query: functionapp.json is our production invoice processor. HTTP p95 is 4.2 s, the Service Bus queue stalls, and we now need the app on the VNet with our SQL server. What do we change?
expected_behavior: States plainly that the `Y1` / `Dynamic` Consumption plan does not support virtual network integration at all, so the VNet requirement is a plan migration and not a setting - and names Flex Consumption as the recommended serverless target because it adds VNet integration while keeping scale-to-zero billing

Attributes the 4.2 s p95 against a 90 ms p50 to cold starts on a plan that scales to zero, and prescribes Flex Consumption always-ready instances (or a Premium plan) rather than `alwaysOn`, which has no effect on a Consumption plan

Notes that Flex Consumption is Linux only, offers 512 / 2048 / 4096 MB instance sizes, and scales to 1000 instances against Consumption's 200, and that all Flex apps in a subscription and region share a default quota of 250 cores
Calls out Node 18 as out of support and names the versions Flex Consumption actually accepts (Node 22 or 24), so the migration is also a runtime upgrade
Identifies the extension bundle range `[2.*, 3.0.0)` as stale for a v4 host and moves it to `[4.*, 5.0.0)`

Replaces the `AzureWebJobsStorage`, Service Bus and SQL connection strings with identity-based connections - `AzureWebJobsStorage__accountName` plus `ServiceBusConnection__fullyQualifiedNamespace` with role assignments - and points out that the app has `identity: null`, so a managed identity has to be enabled first
Says the `WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE` and `WEBSITE_CONTENTAZUREFILECONNECTIONSTRING` settings must be dropped on the way to Flex Consumption, which has a single deployment path and ignores them

Diagnoses the Service Bus stall from the binding configuration - `prefetchCount: 0` with `maxConcurrentCalls: 32` - rather than blaming the queue, and flags `minTlsVersion: 1.0`, `ftpsState: AllAllowed` and `publicNetworkAccess: Enabled` as separate hardening findings
Keeps Application Insights advice to the Azure product surface (sampling is disabled, so ingestion cost scales with traffic) instead of designing an OpenTelemetry instrumentation or alerting pipeline

query: hub_network.tf 里删掉 subnets 变量中的 "data" 之后，plan 显示要销毁重建 mgmt 和 bastion 两个子网，可它们明明没改。为什么？怎么改才安全？
expected_behavior: Answers it as a Terraform resource-identity question: `count` addresses instances by list index, so removing `"data"` shifts `mgmt` from index 2 to 1 and `bastion` from 3 to 2, and every later address is renumbered

Prescribes `for_each` over a keyed collection (for example `toset(var.subnets)`) plus `moved` blocks from `azurerm_subnet.this[N]` to `azurerm_subnet.this["name"]`, and notes that `cidrsubnet(..., count.index)` must become a stable per-key index or the prefixes shift too
Does not turn the answer into Azure control-plane advice about VNets, subscriptions, Bicep or the Azure CLI
skill_read is false for the `azure` skill

query: order-sync is a C# in-process Function App. Management wants it on .NET 10 isolated before the in-process deadline. Using OrderSync.csproj, Functions.cs and deploy-notes.md, give me the migration plan: what changes in the project, the code, the app settings and the rollout, and what could break silently.
expected_behavior: States that in-process support ends on 2026-11-10 and that the fix is the isolated worker model, not a .NET version bump within in-process

Flags that .NET 10 cannot run on Linux Consumption (the app's current plan): either migrate to isolated on .NET 8 first and keep the plan, or treat moving to Flex Consumption as a separate hosting migration (new app, no slots) - it does not plan .NET 10 on the existing Linux Consumption app

Uses `Azure.Functions.Sdk` as the project SDK with an explicit `Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker` reference, removing `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Functions`, `Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Extensions` and the WebJobs Service Bus package in favour of `Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.Extensions.ServiceBus`

Warns that the CI restores the solution, while the Functions project must be restored directly (solution/traversal restore skips the SDK's extension post-restore hook, AZFW0108); does not edit the generated obj/azure_functions.g.csproj

Says System.Text.Json silently ignores the Newtonsoft `[JsonProperty]` names on OrderMessage (fields bind to defaults without an error), so the attributes must become `[JsonPropertyName]` or Newtonsoft must be configured, verified against the existing sample payload

Sets FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME=dotnet-isolated in local.settings.json Values and in the Bicep app settings (not only a shell export), and rolls out by changing the setting and publishing together on the staging slot, then swapping, because the setting/code mismatch fails (AZFD0013) in between

query: activity-log.json has three failed AKS node pool operations from this week and clusters.md has the context. For each one tell me the root cause and the fix. Do not change anything yet.
expected_behavior: For npapps reads ZonalAllocationFailed as missing zonal capacity for that VM size, not a quota problem (quota has headroom), and proposes retrying the upgrade with maxSurge=0 and maxUnavailable greater than 0 (no surge nodes), or another size/zone, as an approval-gated change

For npbatch uses the nested signature, not the outer VMExtensionProvisioningError: VMExtensionError_K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFail / vmssCSE exit 52 means the node cannot resolve the private API server FQDN

Ties exit 52 to the custom DNS chain: the hub DNS servers must forward `privatelink.westeurope.azmk8s.io` (conditional forwarder) to Azure DNS 168.63.129.16 from a VNet linked to the private DNS zone, instead of sending it on-premises; verifies with nslookup of the API FQDN

For npcache explains Standard_D4s_v5 has no local temp/cache disk, so an Ephemeral OS disk cannot fit; the fix is a new node pool with a size that has enough temp storage (for example Standard_D4ds_v5, 150 GiB) or a managed OS disk - OS disk type and size cannot be changed on an existing pool
Points out that the runbook flags (`Standard_D4s_v5` with `--node-osdisk-type Ephemeral`) will fail the same way for anyone else who copies them

query: cluster-state.txt has what both teams sent me. The ERP team says AKS auto-upgrade is broken; the Web team wants their cluster switched to rapid and SecurityPatch. What do I tell each team, and what exactly should change?
expected_behavior: Tells the ERP team auto-upgrade is not broken but off: `upgradeChannel` is `none`, and a maintenance window (aksManagedAutoUpgradeSchedule) only schedules upgrades - it never enables them
Proposes choosing a channel (for example `stable` or `patch`) as the owner's decision, notes channel changes can take up to 24 hours to take effect, and that maintenance runs are best effort
Explains npbatch is Stopped, so upgrades are applied only when the pool starts

Tells the Web team that AKS Automatic fixes the channels (`stable` for the cluster, `NodeImage` for node OS) - they cannot be switched to `rapid` or `SecurityPatch`; only the maintenance windows are configurable, or they need an AKS Standard cluster

query: gpu-state.txt is from our ML cluster. Do what the ML lead asks: cut the GPU bill by deleting workspace-mistral-old, and get llm-chat scheduled. Tell me the exact steps and anything that will not do what he expects.
expected_behavior: Says deleting the KAITO Workspace does not delete the GPU node pool KAITO provisioned for it (one of ws2f9c1a/ws7b30e4), which keeps billing; the matching pool must be identified by the `kaito.sh/workspace` node label and deleted separately

Diagnoses gpua100 as a driver-only GPU profile (`driver: Install`, no managed NVIDIA stack): AKS installed the driver but no device plugin, so nodes advertise no `nvidia.com/gpu` and the pod is Pending

Fixes llm-chat without rebuilding by deploying the NVIDIA device plugin (or GPU Operator) to the pool, and says the gpuProfile fields cannot be changed in place - switching to the AKS-managed stack would require a new node pool
Gates the deletions behind explicit confirmation rather than running them
